rows.text: The distinction that matters is between a single prompt and response and a task an agent sees through to the end. A chatbot that answers one question is not agentic. A system that reads a support ticket, looks up the order, drafts a refund and issues it is agentic. Nobody scripted that exact sequence in advance. Security reviewers and boards ask about it separately from the model itself, because the risk changes once a system can act, not only speak. A wrong sentence in a chat reply is embarrassing. A wrong action against a live order or a payment has already happened by the time anyone notices, because nothing stood between the decision and the outcome.

rows.text: AI governance sits above the technology itself. It covers who owns each AI system, what data it may touch, which use cases are off limits, and who signs off before a system reaches customers. A written answer exists the day a customer or auditor asks for one.

rows.text: GDPR Article 35 makes this review mandatory, not a judgement call, in three situations. One is large-scale profiling with legal or similarly significant effects. Another is large-scale processing of special-category data, such as health or biometric records. The third is systematic large-scale monitoring of a public space. Most consequential AI systems land in the first of these by default. The assessment has to describe the processing and why it is necessary. It has to assess the risk to the people concerned and set out the measures that reduce it. Where the company has appointed a data protection officer, the company must consult that officer while it carries out the assessment. Signing off afterward does not count. Where the system is high-risk under the EU AI Act, Article 26 also refers to the DPIA. A deployer must draw on the information the provider supplies under Article 13 when carrying out this GDPR assessment. The two obligations end up sharing evidence, not separate files.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up Almost any AI system worth building processes personal data, which makes a DPIA the default question rather than an edge case. Legal or procurement asks for it specifically once a system moves from a prototype to something touching real customer records. People often confuse it with the newer AI Act impact assessment. The Article 29 Working Party's 2017 guidelines list criteria that point to high risk. Systematic monitoring is one. Data about vulnerable people is another, and employees may count as vulnerable because of the power imbalance. Meeting two criteria means a DPIA in most cases. Whether a dashboard of AI tool usage counts as systematic monitoring depends on how person-level it is. rows.text: Formally Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Act entered into force on 1 August 2024. It sorts AI systems into a risk ladder, from banned practices, to a high-risk category, to a lighter set of transparency duties. High-risk covers things like hiring, credit and law enforcement. The lighter duties apply to systems such as chatbots. The Act leaves everything else largely unregulated. Obligations scale with the tier. High-risk systems carry duties such as a conformity assessment, technical documentation, human oversight, and registration in an EU database. The Act applies to any company whose AI system is used in the EU, not only companies based there. That is why a US-based startup with European customers cannot treat this as someone else's problem. In practice, the Act changes what "we did not think about that" costs. For a high-risk use case, a company now needs a documented risk assessment and a named point of human oversight. The company also needs evidence of both, ready before a regulator or a customer's legal team asks.

rows.text: The comparison that matters is to an ordinary test suite. There is one difference: the system under test can give a different answer each run. rows.text: A system reaches the category one of two ways. Article 6(1) covers the first: a safety component of a product already regulated under EU product-safety law, or that product itself. Medical devices and machinery are examples. That product-safety law already requires third-party conformity assessment. Annex III covers the second: eight listed use-case areas, among them biometric identification, employment decisions, credit scoring and law enforcement. Article 6(2) makes a system high-risk just by falling into one of those areas, with no product-safety law involved at all. A system inside Annex III can still escape the label under Article 6(3), for four narrow reasons. One is a limited procedural task, such as reformatting an application into a standard template. Another is improving a human decision already made, such as tidying a report's wording without changing its recommendation. A third is detecting a deviation without replacing human judgement, such as flagging an unusual transaction for a fraud analyst to review. The fourth is a preparatory task ahead of someone else's assessment, such as gathering a loan applicant's documents before a human underwriter looks at them. None of the four applies to profiling: a system that profiles individual people is high-risk regardless.

rows.text: The concept sits on a spectrum, from full autonomy at one end to human-in-the-loop at the other. With human-in-the-loop, a person must actively approve each step before it happens. Human-on-the-loop sits in between: a person can intervene but does not have to act. Where a system falls on that spectrum is a design decision, not a fixed property of the technology. For anything that can affect a person's money, employment or legal standing, this decision is one of the first things a customer's security team or a regulator asks about. Article 14 of the EU AI Act requires "effective" human oversight for high-risk systems: oversight that can genuinely catch and correct a bad output, not a person who clicks approve without reading it. In practice, this decides where a company can safely remove a person from a workflow, and where it still needs one.

rows.text: Article 14 splits human oversight into two kinds of measure. The provider builds one kind into the system itself before it ships, such as an interface that flags a low-confidence output. The provider identifies the other kind for the deployer to carry out instead. An example of that kind is a rule about when a person must review a case before it proceeds. Article 14 lists five capacities the overseeing person needs. They must understand the system's real limits well enough to spot a malfunction. They must stay alert to automation bias, the tendency to trust the output by default. They also need to interpret the output correctly and to disregard or reverse a specific output when needed. Last, they need a way to halt the system outright.

rows.text: ISO/IEC's joint technical committee for artificial intelligence wrote it. It specifies requirements for an AI management system: the recurring policies, roles and processes that govern how an organisation develops, provides or uses AI. It uses the same Plan-Do-Check-Act structure as other ISO management-system standards, such as ISO/IEC 27001 for information security. Unlike the NIST AI RMF, a free framework, ISO/IEC 42001 is a standard that an accredited third party can audit and certify a company against. Enterprise customers and procurement teams ask for it, or ask how your company compares with it. They ask because certification gives them a documented, externally checked answer instead of a vendor's own claim. Working towards the standard means three things: writing down a risk-assessment method, running an inventory of AI systems, and reviewing that inventory on a schedule. None of that requires certification itself.

Rank the missing ones by what a customer or auditor would ask about first. The result is a work list, not a certificate and not a pass or fail grade. rows.text: Every call to any model passes through one place, instead of going straight from application code to a vendor's API. A company can then control who may call a model, and log every prompt and response for an audit trail. It can also redact sensitive data before it leaves the building. It can apply rate and cost limits, and fail over to a different provider if one goes down. Without a gateway, API keys end up scattered across a codebase, and nobody holds a full log of what the company sent to a vendor. A data leak through a prompt stays invisible until a customer or regulator finds it first. Engineering teams adopt one to stop rebuilding the same authentication and logging code in every project that touches a model. It also gives a direct, specific answer to a vendor questionnaire's question about how the company controls model access. That beats a description of several applications each doing it inconsistently.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up A security questionnaire almost always asks how the company controls and logs access to the model provider. "Each team manages its own API key" is a poor answer. A board or customer asks a version of the same question after a well-publicised leak elsewhere. In that leak, a prompt carrying sensitive data reached a third-party model unlogged. Without a gateway, nobody can produce every prompt sent to a vendor last month. ## What to do about it Put one gateway in front of every model call before adding a second application that talks to a model, not after. Route all API keys through it rather than into individual codebases, and log every request and response. Redact anything that looks like a customer identifier or a secret before it leaves. Solid open-source and hosted options already exist, so this is rarely worth building in house. ## The gateway as a governance control A written policy says what staff may do with a model. A gateway is the control that enforces it, because every model call passes through one place where the policy runs. It decides who may call which model, strips sensitive data before it leaves, applies rate limits, and logs each request and response. That log is the evidence a security questionnaire asks for: it shows the policy ran, not only that it exists. The limit is coverage: a gateway controls only the calls that go through it, so an application that calls a vendor directly sits outside the control. The [LLM Gateway Governance Config](/resources/llm-gateway-governance-config) gives a policy file format for one.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up In this site's reading, it comes up when a team connects an [agentic workflow](/glossary/agentic-workflow) to its own systems and a security reviewer asks what the agent can touch. "Open protocol" can sound like a safety claim. It is not one. A 2026 sheet from the US National Security Agency (NSA) says MCP's security posture "remains uneven and highly dependent on implementation discipline rather than protocol guarantees". The sheet cites the November 2025 revision of the specification. ## What to do about it The model picks which tool to call, and text it reads can steer that choice. That is [prompt injection](/glossary/prompt-injection). The MCP project's security policy says a report that an LLM invoked an unexpected tool is not an MCP vulnerability. So the limits go in the host and the servers, as [guardrails](/glossary/guardrails) in code. Give each server only the access its task needs. That is least privilege. The NSA sheet recommends that tool execution be constrained and sandboxed. I start every new tool read-only. Any action that writes, spends money or touches personal data needs approval from a named person. Credentials live with the [gateway](/glossary/llm-gateway) or the server, never in the prompt, and they rotate every quarter. ## Before a third-party server connects I pin the exact version of a third-party server and review its source before it connects. The approved-server list lives in the client's [AI register](/glossary/ai-register). ## Where the specification stops The specification, in its 28 July 2026 revision, names who should do the first three jobs. The protocol does not check that anyone does. - Approval before a tool runs: the host. There should always be a [human in the loop](/glossary/human-in-the-loop) who can deny a call. - Checks on inputs and access: each server. Servers must validate all tool inputs and implement proper access controls. - Logs: the host's clients. They should log tool usage, which feeds [observability](/glossary/observability). MCP traffic goes through the gateway. The call and the result are logged, never the full arguments, and the log is kept for 90 days. The log is reviewed in the weekly ops check. - Local servers: a local server the client starts runs with the client's privileges. The policy says the SDK's STDIO transport, which does the starting, "is not a sandbox". Local STDIO servers run inside a container by default. Remote HTTP is used only through the gateway, with authentication. ## What the client receives The server inventory and the approved-server list land in the client's AI register. This work is part of the two-week [AI readiness and risk assessment](/services/ai-readiness-and-risk-assessment). ## When I review this entry Last reviewed: 7 October 2026. I review this entry again on every new revision of the specification and on any new class of CVE.

rows.text: The format comes from a 2018 paper. The paper proposed model cards as a response to models shipping with no consistent account of how their makers had actually tested them. A rigorous card reports evaluation broken out by group: race, geographic location, sex, skin type. It also breaks out intersections, such as age combined with race, instead of one blended figure that hides where performance drops. NIST's risk management framework expects the same thing in substance. A model should be explained, validated and documented, not simply shipped. A vendor who has actually done that evaluation work typically wants to show the results, since they usually help on some axis. One who cannot produce a card has most likely skipped the evaluation itself, not just the paperwork describing it.

rows.text: Article 53 of the EU AI Act turned this from a private claim into a published one for general-purpose models. Providers must publish a sufficiently detailed summary of training content, following a template the AI Office issued. That summary covers the scale of the data, and whether it includes licensed material, scraped web content, user data or synthetic data. For a smaller company building on someone else's model, provenance is a due-diligence question, not a publishing duty. Work through it before signing, not after. That distinction decides who actually reads the summary, and when. The company reads the summary before it signs a contract, not after a customer's legal team goes looking for where the data came from.

rows.text: The framework sets out four functions an organisation applies to an AI system. GOVERN covers policy and accountability, while MAP covers understanding context and risk. Testing and metrics fall under MEASURE. Acting on what it found is MANAGE's job. It is not a law, and it is not sector specific. A bank, a hospital and a ten-person startup can all use the same structure. US procurement teams, and increasingly non-US ones, ask about it. They ask because the framework gives a common vocabulary for a question that used to have no fixed answer. That question is how you know your company actually manages an AI system's risks, not just discusses them once. In practice, adopting the framework means someone can point to a specific function, and to a specific piece of evidence behind it. That beats a general assurance that everything is under control.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up It comes up in almost every vendor security questionnaire, and in board packs once a company runs more than one AI system. A customer's risk team wants a framework they recognise, not a bespoke description of your process. They want it because it lets them compare you against every other vendor they review. rows.text: An agentic workflow is a system that also calls tools to look things up or take actions on its own. Its record has to extend further. rows.text: Direct injection comes from whoever is typing into the box, phrased to override the model's own hidden starting instructions, its system prompt. Indirect injection is the more dangerous form. It arrives inside content the model retrieves on its own: a webpage it is summarising, a resume it is screening. No attacker ever touches the model directly. Multimodal systems add a further variant, since an instruction can hide inside an image processed alongside ordinary text. It has kept that position through every edition of the list, most recently the 2026 revision. The reason is structural: the model reads instructions and untrusted data through the same channel. A filter tuned on known patterns still misses a novel phrasing. Every mitigation available today reduces the odds of a successful attack; none removes them.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up It is the first thing a security reviewer probes on any AI feature that reads outside content. That means a webpage, an uploaded file, an email, or a customer's own message history. The concern is not academic. A model that can also send an email, issue a refund or query a database turns a successful injection into something already done. It is no longer just an embarrassing reply. ## What to do about it Never let a model's output directly trigger a sensitive action without a check enforced in code. Keep the model's own permissions to the smallest set it needs. Treat anything the model reads from outside the conversation as untrusted input, the way a web application treats a user-supplied string. Evals for exactly this kind of attack belong in the same pipeline that gates every other change. That is how I structure the [90-Day Production Sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint).

rows.text: Article 3 defines a provider by two acts done together. The first is developing the system, or having someone else develop it. The second is placing it on the market or putting it into service, under the provider's own name or trademark. Payment is irrelevant. A company that fine-tunes a vendor's model and ships the result under its own product name has made itself the provider of that product. It does not matter that it built none of the underlying model. Owning the brand is what matters, not how much of the system the company actually wrote.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up It surfaces in a contract negotiation once both sides realise the label matters more than expected. A provider owes technical documentation and a conformity assessment, while a deployer mainly owes human oversight and monitoring. A board hears about it when a vendor's contract quietly assigns the company duties it assumed the vendor carried. Getting the role wrong can leave a company holding an obligation nobody budgeted for. ## What to do about it Run the provider-or-deployer test per system, not per company. Rebranding one vendor's model can make a company a provider for that product while it stays a deployer for everything else it merely uses. Write the answer into the AI register alongside the risk tier, since a security questionnaire will eventually ask for both. The [Fractional CAIO Retainer](/services/fractional-caio-retainer) is where I answer this kind of question inside a live negotiation. ## Deployer obligations checklist Article 26 of the EU AI Act sets these duties for a deployer of a [high-risk AI system](/glossary/high-risk-ai-system). They apply to high-risk systems only. The provider carries a separate set of duties, and public authorities and some biometric uses carry further duties in the same Article. - Use the system as the provider's instructions for use say. - Assign [human oversight](/glossary/human-oversight) to people who have the competence, training, authority and support to do it. - Make sure the input data you control is relevant and representative for the system's purpose. - Monitor the system against those instructions. If you have reason to think it presents a risk, tell the provider, importer or distributor and the market surveillance authority without undue delay, and suspend its use. - Report a [serious incident](/glossary/serious-incident-reporting) at once, to the provider first. - Keep the logs the system generates, as far as you control them, for at least six months unless other law says otherwise. - If you are an employer, tell the workers' representatives and the affected workers before you use a high-risk system at work. - Tell people when a high-risk system listed in Annex III makes or helps make a decision about them. - Use the provider's information for your [data protection impact assessment](/glossary/dpia) where one is required. - Cooperate with the competent authorities.

rows.text: A red team engagement produces a different kind of output than a test run. It is a list of the specific techniques that worked, detailed enough for someone else to reproduce the failure. It also carries a judgement on what an attacker could actually do with it. That reproducibility is what separates a report from an anecdote about something that broke once. NIST's generative AI profile recommends red teaming as a check against specific categories of harm, including information leakage and harmful content generation. Those failures depend on someone actively trying to cause them; they rarely show up in ordinary use. The finding that matters is the one nobody predicted going in.

rows.text: The document store is usually a vector index. The system converts passages into embeddings, numerical representations of meaning, and matches a query against them by similarity, not exact keyword. Matching on meaning lets the system find a relevant passage even when the question shares none of the same words as the document. OWASP, the group that publishes widely used security-risk lists, tracks this as its own risk category. In a shared vector database, one customer's data can leak into another customer's results. Embeddings carry a second risk: someone can sometimes invert them to recover the source text they came from. Both risks sit inside the retrieval layer, invisible to anyone reviewing only the model or the prompts it receives.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up Procurement asks "is this RAG, or did you train on our data," because the two have different data-handling implications. RAG typically sends only retrieved snippets to the model at query time, rather than baking a customer's content into the model's own weights. It also comes up once someone questions accuracy. rows.text: GDPR Article 28 calls the AI vendor the processor and your company the controller. It gives the processor two ways to add a sub-processor. Specific authorisation names the sub-processor up front, so the controller signs off by name. General authorisation lets the processor add sub-processors as needed, but it has to tell the controller first and give a real chance to object. Either way, the processor must pass down the same data-protection obligations it owes directly, in the contract itself, not just a notice. The chain does not stop at one level either. The processor often runs its own infrastructure through a further sub-processor, such as a cloud host or a fine-tuning partner. That passes the same flow-down obligation another level down. Asking for the sub-processor list is really asking how many hops sit between a company's data and the last party that can actually see it.

rows.text: The EU AI Act sets the content directly in Annex IV, rather than leaving it to the provider's judgement. A national authority or notified body has to be able to assess it without relying on the provider's own explanation. Article 11 lets a small or micro enterprise use a simplified version of the same form, one the Commission publishes for that purpose. Article 18 sets how long to keep it: ten years from when the provider places the system on the market or puts it into service. A national competent authority can request it at any point in that window. The same retention duty covers the quality management system records and the EU declaration of conformity too, not the technical documentation alone.

rows.text: ## Why it comes up It is different from a marketing spec sheet or an engineering wiki page. A regulator or notified body wants the specific content the Act lists, not a general description of the product. It also comes up in procurement due diligence, where a buyer of a high-risk system sometimes asks to see excerpts before signing. A vendor who can produce none of it has told you something. ## What to do about it Start the document on the first day of build, recording design decisions as you make them. Reconstructing the reasoning behind a choice months later is far harder than writing it down at the time. Version it alongside the system itself, so the documentation for a given release actually matches what shipped. The [AI Governance Starter Kit](/resources/ai-governance-starter-kit) covers the register and policy this documentation builds on, ahead of the deeper regulatory detail.

rows.text: In July 2025, METR published a randomised trial. Sixteen experienced open-source developers worked on 246 issues. Before the trial they expected AI to make them 24% faster. Afterwards they believed it had made them 20% faster. Their tasks took 19% longer with AI allowed. METR now marks that result as out of date. That gap between what the developers believed and what the trial found is the subject of this article. In my reading, a dashboard built on self-report inherits it, and no cited source shows usage counts predicting a result. Because METR marks the result as out of date, take the lesson as one about method. It is not a lesson about the size of any one effect. Executives report little effect, and that is also self-report. An NBER working paper issued in February 2026 surveyed nearly 6,000 senior executives in the US, UK, Germany and Australia. It found that 69% of firms use AI. Nine in ten executives reported no impact on employment or productivity over three years. ## How far apart can belief and evidence be? Faros, a vendor, found that teams with high adoption completed 21% more tasks and merged 98% more pull requests, with 91% longer review time and no significant link to company-level improvement. Its data is observational. | | Acceptance rate | Suggestions taken. | In a 2022 preprint on Copilot users, it tracked how productive users said they felt, rather than how long the accepted code lasted. | | Vendor hours saved and ROI | Action counts times fixed minutes times a wage. | Microsoft builds assisted hours from action counts, fixed minutes per action, and meeting recaps counted by meeting length. The research behind this article found no independent study that tests whether a usage-based adoption metric predicts outcomes. ## What should adoption telemetry measure instead? This set is a synthesis of the evidence above. No source states it in these words. Sort every number by where it came from. Logs show what people did. Surveys show what people said. The [evals in CI article](/blog/evals-in-ci-for-llm-agents) covers testing a change before it ships. Adoption telemetry asks whether people keep using the system. ## How do you tell whether it worked? Agree the outcome before rollout. Read it from the system that already records it, such as ticketing, CI or your CRM, and not from the AI tool's own logs. I hand them the question set. Do not rely on staff consent. The Article 29 Working Party's 2017 opinion said consent is highly unlikely to be a legal basis for data processing at work. Paid versus active and retention become two panels, and the survey splits into trust and policy clarity. Each panel names the question it answers, the data source and the decision it supports. rows.text: An AI acceptable use policy only earns its place once it decides who approves a new AI tool and which data tier may reach which category of vendor. Beyond that, it decides whether a person checks AI output before it reaches a customer or a contract. It also decides when the company must tell a customer they are dealing with an AI system. Most templates answer the first two questions and stay quiet on the rest. That is exactly why staff read them once and then ignore them. A policy this size needs one named owner, not a committee. It also needs a review interval short enough to catch the tool people started using without asking. ISO/IEC 42001 treats a policy like this as one part of a management system, not a standalone document. The EU AI Act already requires disclosure once an AI system talks to a customer directly. Skip the enforcement clause and none of the rest holds.

rows.text: Most companies between 30 and 300 people already have staff using AI tools, whether or not a policy says so. The policy that works is not the longest one. It states which data may go where, who approves a new tool, and what happens when someone gets it wrong. It does this in language a new hire reads in one sitting. ## What does a working AI acceptable use policy actually need to say? A policy that survives contact with real staff decides a short list of things, not a long one. Nine sections make up a working one. Each row here names the section, the decision it forces, and the specific failure it exists to prevent. | Section | What it decides | Failure it prevents | | --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Scope | Which staff, contractors and AI tools the policy covers. | A contractor or a new hire assuming the rules do not apply to them. | | Data classification | Which data tier may reach which category of AI vendor. | Client or personal data pasted into a public chatbot with no data agreement. | | Approved tools and requests | Which AI systems are pre-approved, and how staff add another one. | Staff picking an unapproved tool because asking takes too long. | | Human review | Whether a person checks AI output before it reaches a customer, a contract or a filing. | An unreviewed AI draft going out under someone's name. | | Customer disclosure | When the company must tell a customer they are talking to an AI system or seeing AI-made content. | A hidden AI interaction reaching a customer where disclosure is a legal duty. | | Vendor training use | Whether a vendor may use company or client input to train its own models. | Confidential input quietly improving a vendor's public model. | | Ownership and review | Who owns the policy, and how often it is checked against what staff actually use. | A policy that describes a tool nobody uses, and stays silent about the one everyone does. | | Incident reporting | What staff do the moment an AI system produces something wrong or exposes data. | A bad output or a leak going unreported because nobody knew who to tell. | | Enforcement | What happens after a breach, and who decides. | A rule everyone knows the company never actually enforces. | The customer disclosure row is not optional once a system talks to people outside the company. Article 50 of the EU AI Act already requires a provider or a deployer to tell a person they are interacting with an AI system. It also requires labelling content the system generated, whether or not that system counts as high-risk. A staff-facing policy has to name who checks that duty before a customer-facing AI feature ships. The policy must not leave that to whoever built the feature to remember. ## What should the policy refuse to try to do? A policy that tries to be the technical control fails twice. It fails once because a paragraph of text cannot stop a paste into a browser. It fails again because staff read that overreach as proof the whole document is for show. Access limits, contract terms and vendor settings do the technical work. The policy states the rule those controls exist to support. Listing every approved tool by name reads as complete on the day you publish it. It is wrong within weeks, because a new model or a new vendor account always arrives faster than a document gets updated. A policy built around named tools also implies that anything missing from the list is quietly fine, and a reviewer wants to see the opposite. An outright ban is the easiest policy to write and the least effective one to run. It does not remove the reason someone went looking for an AI tool in the first place. It just moves that search out of sight, where it is much harder to see or govern. ## What do you do about the tools staff are already using? By the time you draft a policy, some staff are already using AI without asking anyone first. That means drafting client emails in a personal chatbot account or running a browser extension nobody vetted. It also means building a habit around a coding assistant they picked themselves. That is [shadow AI](/glossary/shadow-ai), and treating it as rare is the first mistake a policy can make. Two moves fix more of it than a warning email does. First, make the approved path faster than the workaround: a fast yes for a low-risk tool beats a slow review nobody wants to wait for. Second, check instead of asking. Checking browser extensions, expense claims and what the company actually pays AI vendors shows what people are really running. That beats trusting a self-reported survey. ## What happens when someone breaks the policy? Most breaches are not sabotage. Someone pastes a client's contract into a personal chatbot account to move faster, not to leak it. That is different from someone who was told a tool was blocked and used it anyway, or who hid AI involvement in work they signed off as their own. A policy that cannot tell the two apart will punish the wrong case or excuse the real one. One named role decides what happens next. That is the same person who owns the AI register and the policy itself, not a group chat and not a vote. They classify what happened and decide whether legal or an affected client needs to hear about it. They also choose the response, from a conversation to removal of access to company systems. That decision runs through the disciplinary process HR already has for any other policy breach. The AI policy needs a clear point where that existing process starts, not a punishment system of its own. Silence is its own answer too. If a policy never states what happens after a breach, staff test it once and learn from the result whether any of it is real. ## Who should own it, and how does it stay current? The same person who is already accountable for AI risk overall should hold this document. A shared inbox cannot hold it, because someone has to be answerable when a customer or an auditor asks a direct question. [ISO/IEC 42001](/glossary/iso-iec-42001) treats a policy like this as one part of a management system, reviewed on a schedule and checked against a live inventory. A review interval only works if you tie it to something that actually changes. That can be a new hire, a new vendor account, or a client contract that names a data rule of its own. Quarterly is a reasonable default for a company this size. The exact interval matters less than the fact that one exists and someone is accountable for keeping it. The version I run for my own practice is public at [my AI policy](/ai-policy). It is one page, a worked example of the same shape at a much smaller scale. The [Starter Kit](/resources/ai-governance-starter-kit) lists the documents a security review asks for and who signs each. It suits a company with more than one person to coordinate. ## What doesn't a policy like this solve? A written policy does not tell you whether anyone inside the company actually owns AI risk today. If nobody does, there is no obvious person to hand the draft to. So the gap usually surfaces during an [AI readiness and risk assessment](/services/ai-readiness-and-risk-assessment), before it ever reaches the policy stage. Someone determined to break the rule will do it regardless; no policy stops that. A policy removes the excuse of not knowing, and it gives the company a fair, defensible reason to act when someone crosses the line anyway. Nobody enforces it without an owner, a review date and a stated consequence. Skip those and it is a page people skim once and never open again.

rows.text: Evals in CI put a fixed test set on every prompt, model, or code change. The build fails when the pass rate drops. A regression gets caught before a reviewer approves the pull request, not after a customer notices. Build the set from real production traffic. Sample across a period long enough that one quiet week does not flatter the result. Most agent tasks have no single correct answer. Score them in layers instead. Start with deterministic checks: a tool call shape, a required field, a data format. Add a reference-free judge for whether an answer is grounded in what the agent retrieved. Fall back to a comparison against the last known-good version for everything else. Treat the judge as a component that needs calibration against a human-labelled sample, not as ground truth. A cost ceiling per completed run sits in the same job as the score. An expensive change then fails the build for the same reason a wrong one does.

rows.text: An eval suite that only runs on a laptop protects nobody. The same regression a developer catches by eye on a good day slips through on a bad one. A model provider's silent update slips through every time. Putting [an eval suite](/glossary/evals) in CI turns a habit into a gate. The pull request cannot merge until the numbers clear, whoever is watching. ## How do you build an eval set from production traffic? Pull the first cases from what the agent has actually handled, not from what a spec said it should handle. Real traces carry the phrasing, the edge cases, and the odd multi-step requests. A person writing test data from imagination never thinks to include them. A support agent's eval set should read like a week of its own transcripts, because that is exactly what it is. Sample across a period long enough that one good or bad week does not decide the result. A month of traffic spans weekdays, weekends, and spikes the business already expects, which is a sturdier base than one convenient week. Mix the set on purpose. Include three kinds of case: routine ones that should always pass, a handful known to be hard, and a few with no single acceptable answer. Most agent tasks in production fall into that last kind. Store the set next to the code it tests, in a format a reviewer can read in a pull request. Change it through the same review a code change gets. Revisit the set on a fixed schedule rather than whenever someone remembers. Retire a case once the product has genuinely outgrown it. Add one the day a new failure reaches production. That keeps the set tracking how people actually use the agent. ## How do you score an agent when there is no golden answer? Most agent tasks do not reduce to one correct string, so do not force them into that shape. A support reply, a summary, or a multi-step tool sequence can be right in more than one way. A scorer built for exact match will reject good answers as often as it catches bad ones. Score in layers instead, cheapest and most reliable checks first. Start with deterministic checks on anything mechanical. Check whether the agent called the right tool, with a valid argument set, in a shape that downstream code can actually parse. These checks are cheap, and they never disagree with themselves. In most agentic systems, they catch a large share of regressions before a judge ever runs. OWASP's list of risks in large language model applications names excessive agency as one of the standard failure modes worth testing for. Excessive agency means an agent taking an action its task never asked for. Write a case for every tool the agent can call. Each case should check that the tool stays quiet when not needed, and that it fires correctly when needed. For the answer's content, add a reference-free judge. Look at the question and whatever the agent actually retrieved. Then check whether every claim in the answer traces back to a document it had in hand. This catches a fluent, confident answer that is not supported by anything the system looked at. A plain accuracy score misses that failure mode entirely. Where no rubric fits cleanly, fall back to a comparison against the last known-good version. Show a judge both outputs, blind to which one is new, and ask it to pick a winner. A judge finds picking a winner easier than defending an absolute score out of some invented scale. A win rate against a fixed baseline is also a steadier number to watch than a score with no anchor. NIST's AI RMF frames this as a selection problem under its Measure function. Which method fits depends on what is actually being measured. A team documents why it chose a metric, and which ones it rejected. That team ends up with a sturdier suite than one that picked whatever was easiest to compute. ## What happens when the judge itself is flaky? A judge model can score the same input differently on two runs, especially at a higher temperature. That alone will make a pipeline look unstable, even when the agent under test has not changed. Set the judge's own temperature as low as the provider allows. Treat any remaining run-to-run disagreement as a property of the judge to manage. Calibrate the judge on a fixed schedule against a small set of cases a human has already scored. The number that matters is agreement between the judge and the human reviewers. A judge that is consistent but consistently wrong is worse than one that is honestly uncertain. Consistent wrongness hides the problem instead of showing it. Let the judge decline a case it cannot confidently assess. A skipped case should fall out of the pass-rate calculation, rather than count as either a pass or a fail. A case the judge skips often is telling you the rubric does not cover that situation yet. When one specific case flips between pass and fail on identical re-runs, treat that case as broken, not the whole gate. Quarantine it. Keep it running so you can see it, stop it from blocking a merge, and put a name against fixing its rubric or its sampling. Only then should it rejoin the set that actually gates a build. ## What should the pipeline check, and what does a failing check do to the build? Not every check should carry the same weight. A wrong tool call and a slow response are both real problems, but only one of them should stop a release. The table below is the shape of a working gate. It shows what each row measures, how it gets a number, and what that number does to the build when it fails. | What to score | How to score it | What a failing score does to the build | | ---------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Task success on labelled cases | Exact match or a deterministic rule against a known-good answer. | Blocks the merge immediately, with no override. | | Task success with no golden answer | A rubric-based judge scores the answer against stated criteria, not against a reference. | Blocks the merge once the pass rate drops below the floor set for that task. | | Faithfulness to retrieved context | A reference-free judge checks whether each claim traces back to a document the agent actually retrieved. | Blocks the merge; an unsupported claim counts as a defect, not a style note. | | Preference against the last good version | Pairwise comparison: the judge sees both outputs, blind to which is new, and picks a winner. | Blocks the merge if the new version loses on more cases than the agreed margin allows. | | Tool-call correctness | Deterministic check that the agent called the right tool with a valid, schema-checked argument set. | Blocks the merge; a malformed call fails loudly instead of degrading quietly. | | Judge-human agreement | Re-run the rubric against a human-labelled sample on a fixed schedule and compare agreement. | Does not block a single pull request; a drop pages the eval owner to fix the rubric. | | Cost per completed run | Sum of model and tool cost across the eval set, divided by cases completed. | Blocks the merge once the run exceeds the ceiling set in the pipeline config. | | Response time under load | Wall-clock time per case, measured in the same job as the scores. | Warns on the pull request; blocks only if it breaches the budget agreed with the product owner. | ## Where does the cost ceiling sit? Put a cost ceiling in the same job as the quality score. Do not put it on a separate dashboard someone checks once a week. Agent systems fail commercially long before they fail technically. Consider a tool call that retries a few times on a bad response: harmless in a demo, ruinous once real traffic hits it. Measure cost per completed run, across the whole eval set, the way you measure the pass rate. A change that makes the agent slower or more expensive without a real gain is a regression, even if every other score stays green. A [90-Day Production Sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint) puts this gate in place before a workflow takes its first real user. That is a cheaper time to find the problem than after the first invoice. ## What does the pipeline do when a check fails? A failing check blocks the merge by default. The pull request gets a summary next to the diff that caused it. That summary lists which cases failed, what the agent returned, and what the check expected. Nobody reconstructs the failure from a log. Not every failure deserves the same response. A wrong tool call or an unsupported claim should stop the release outright. A latency or cost warning close to its budget, or a drop in judge-human agreement, can page an owner instead, without stopping every other change in the queue. Keep that distinction explicit in the pipeline config, not in someone's memory of which checks are actually load-bearing. Only a named reviewer, not the author of the change, can override a hard block. That override has to write itself into the same log the eval results live in. An override that leaves no trace is indistinguishable from no gate at all. It gets used that way the next time someone is in a hurry.

rows.text: To hand over AI leadership to an internal owner, move the role in steps and finish with a test. Name one owner early, usually the tech lead or the head of data. My handover takes three months: two side by side, then one led by the new owner. The final test and the signatures come at the end of month three. Three checks close it, and I judge each one. The new owner writes an eval case, runs a rollback rehearsal and handles one incident without me in the room. Until the handover date I sign risk acceptances and the customer security questionnaires that carry my name. After that the internal owner signs. For thirty days after the last day I answer questions by email within one working day and hold one review call on day 30. No engagement has yet ended in a full handover by this method. Searches in October 2026 found no standard, law or study on how to hand over AI leadership.

rows.text: An outside AI lead sets up governance or ships a first system. Sooner or later the role has to sit with someone on the payroll. Four questions run through a handover: what moves, who takes the role, who signs what, and how the company knows it worked. ## Is there a standard way to hand over AI leadership? None turned up. In October 2026, searches of standards bodies, regulators and journals found no standard, law or study on this exact move. What exists sits next door. Interim and fractional executives have exit practices. Engineering teams have ways to transfer ownership of a service. A UK financial regulator has rules for handing over a senior role. The [NIST AI RMF](/glossary/nist-ai-rmf) and the [EU AI Act](/glossary/eu-ai-act) texts checked in October 2026 never mention a change of person. The evidence is thin. [One academic model of interim assignments](https://doi.org/10.1108/JOEPP-10-2019-0094) says the evidence base on interim effectiveness lacks empirical studies. A company linked to two of its authors funded its literature search. Most checklists come from firms that sell interim or fractional staff. Read what follows as practice that others found sensible, plus some points that have no outside source. None of it is proven. ## What has to move in a handover? Documents alone can fall short. [Esya](https://esya.studio/notes/ai-evals-runbook-handover), a UK studio that builds AI inside client companies, writes that a folder of documents can be complete while the handover is not. It says the receiving team also needs the route to deploy and controlled access to systems. It needs monitoring data, the [evals](/glossary/evals) and the runbook. It needs authority over incidents and practised knowledge. Esya sells related work, so read that as a peer's view. The table shows what each source asks for, and how much weight it can bear. Six rows come from sources about handovers, exits or onboarding. The three NIST rows are marked. The NIST text checked in October 2026 never mentions a change of person, so applying it to a handover is this page's reading. | What moves | What a source asks for | The source and its weight | | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Decisions and reasons. | Handover material should include judgement and opinion, not just facts and figures. | [UK Financial Conduct Authority handbook](https://handbook.fca.org.uk/handbook/sysc25/sysc25s9). Regulator guidance for UK financial firms, so an analogy only. | | Work in progress. | A status report on the goals set at the start: what got done, what remains and what new issues emerged. | [CompassPoint](https://www.compasspoint.org/sites/default/files/documents/Interim%20EDs%20-%20final.pdf). A practitioner's guide to interim directors of US nonprofits. | | The list of AI systems. | Mechanisms to inventory AI systems. | [NIST AI RMF](https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/airmf/5-sec-core/), Govern 1.6. A voluntary framework that NIST says it is revising. Not about handovers: this row is the page's reading. | | Roles and authority. | Roles, responsibilities and lines of communication for mapping, measuring and managing AI risks are documented and clear to individuals and teams throughout the organisation. | NIST AI RMF, Govern 2.1. Voluntary. Not about handovers: this row is the page's reading. | | How to run and change the system. | The route to deploy, monitoring data, the evals, a runbook and authority over incidents. | Esya. A studio that sells related work. | | Access. | Revoke access in one coordinated step on or before the last day, and confirm it in writing. | [Fractionus](https://fractionus.com/blog/fractional-executive-offboarding). A marketplace that sells fractional executives, so one vendor's opinion. | | Monitoring and incident duty. | Monitoring plans that cover incident response, recovery and change management. | NIST AI RMF, Manage 4.1. Voluntary. Not about handovers: this row is the page's reading. | | Someone to ask. | The development team must be available to back up and advise the receiving team while it settles. | [Google's SRE book](https://sre.google/sre-book/evolving-sre-engagement-model/). The operator's own account of its engineering teams. | | A report on how it went. | An exit review that names the issues the client needs to address. | [Institute of Interim Management code](https://iim.org.uk/resources/code-of-conduct/). A professional body's code for UK interim managers. | Nine rows are a lot to move on one day. Google's book describes a progressive transfer of responsibilities and ownership, including parts of operations, the change management process and access rights. This page reads that as support for moving a handover in steps. My access list has six categories: the [AI register](/glossary/ai-register), the [LLM gateway](/glossary/llm-gateway), CI/CD, the cloud consoles, the vendor panels and the SSO admin. The client's internal owner or IT lead revokes each one. Revocation is confirmed in writing the same day. A revoke-all line sits on the last-day checklist. ## Who should take the role? The company side needs one named person with the authority to pause the system. The [pilot article](/blog/why-your-ai-pilot-never-reached-production) says the same. It adds that the person should have written at least one eval case and watched a rollback rehearsal. Someone who was not part of the build inherits a document, not an understanding. The usual successor is the tech lead or the head of data. A COO takes the role when AI sits deep in company processes. One person holds the role. This site's own pages point to two jobs inside the role. One is answering for risk, including the authority to stop a launch. The other is keeping the system working, including the eval case and the rollback rehearsal. One person holds both jobs. [NIST's playbook](https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/playbook/govern/) suggests managing development apart from testing, so that someone can correct a system independently of its builders. That is about testing, not owners, but it shows why a company might split the jobs. A US federal memo from April 2025 makes a different choice. The chief information officer is one example, if that person has significant expertise in AI. The memo binds US federal agencies only, so for a private company it is an analogy. It also requires agencies to tell the Office of Management and Budget within thirty days when the officer changes or the post is vacant. Later revisions were not checked. Sometimes nobody inside can take the role yet. The academic paper cited earlier notes that recruiting a senior executive can take six months or more. That figure is not specific to AI roles. No competence framework for a chief AI officer or head of AI from a standards body or regulator turned up in the search. The test the new owner must pass has to be written locally. ## How do you know the handover worked? Test behaviour, not paperwork. [Google's SRE book](https://sre.google/sre-book/evolving-sre-engagement-model/) says a production readiness review is considered a prerequisite for a site reliability team to accept responsibility for the production side of a service. So the receiving side sets a bar before it takes ownership. That is a reading of the text. A specialist team can refuse a service that fails the review. A single internal owner may lack that power, so agree the check with the outside lead in advance. Esya's test is short: the receiving team has practised the response and can make the next change without waiting for the builders to return. Some checks already appear on this site. The pilot article says the new owner should have written at least one eval case and watched a rollback rehearsal. The [approach page](/approach) lists a related measure under engineering capability. It tests whether your engineers can already roll back a bad model without waiting on the outside lead. Three checks close my handover, and I judge each one. The new owner writes an eval case. The new owner runs a rollback rehearsal. The new owner handles one incident without me in the room. Write the full list of checks with the outside lead before the handover starts. rows.text: A security review of an AI system usually starts with one question: what is actually running. If the honest answer takes a week of digging through chat logs and old tickets, the review stalls before it reaches architecture or data flows. An AI system register is the fix: one document listing every AI system a company runs, who owns it, and how risky it is. ## What is an AI system register? An AI system register is the full inventory of every AI system a company runs, regardless of how it got there. That includes a customer-facing feature and an internal copilot. It also includes a marketing tool with a model switched on inside it that nobody called an AI project when they signed up. A working entry names what the system does, what data can reach it, and which vendor or model sits behind it. It also names who owns it and a rough risk tier. Some call this same list an [AI register](/glossary/ai-register) rather than an AI system register. Most of the systems on the list never started as a formal AI project. That is why the list has to go looking for them rather than wait to be told. ## Why does a security reviewer ask for it before anything else? A security or procurement reviewer asks one version of the same question first: what touches our data. Without a register, answering that means paging engineering, marketing, finance and support one by one, and hoping nobody forgot a tool. The [NIST AI RMF](/glossary/nist-ai-rmf) treats this as a named control, not a nice extra. Its Govern function includes a specific requirement: a mechanism to inventory AI systems, resourced according to how much risk the organisation is willing to carry. Everything a reviewer asks next, a data flow diagram, a vendor contract clause, an incident plan, gets scoped against rows already on this list. Skip the register, and the reviewer either stalls the process or signs off on a system nobody can fully describe. ## What should the register record? A register only earns its keep if a reviewer can answer their own questions from it, without a follow-up meeting. What follows is close to the version I hand a client. It has enough fields to answer a first review, and no field that exists only to look thorough. | What to record | Why a reviewer wants it | Who fills it in | | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Name the system and what it does. | A reviewer cannot scope a check against a system they cannot picture. | The system's product or engineering owner. | | Note whether the company built it in-house or bought it, and which vendor or model sits behind it. | A vendor's own controls become part of the risk the moment its API touches your data. | Whoever set up the account or the integration. | | List the data the system can see. | This sets the risk tier and decides which contract terms and legal duties actually apply. | The team that owns the data source, with legal signing off. | | Record who relies on the system's output. | Blast radius matters as much as data sensitivity when a reviewer decides how much scrutiny to apply. | The system owner, from usage or team headcount. | | Mark its deployment status: pilot, production or retired. | A pilot running on sample data is a different conversation from a live system holding real customer records. | The system owner, kept current as status changes. | | Name one internal owner. | A reviewer wants a person who can answer for the system, not a distribution list nobody reads. | Whoever runs the team that operates the system. | | Assign a risk tier. | This decides how much documentation, testing and sign-off the reviewer expects before anything ships. | Whoever runs the security or risk review, not the system's own owner. | | Log the date it was last checked. | A register that has not moved in a year gets treated the same as no register at all. | Whoever owns the register process, on a fixed schedule. | ## How do you build one in a week without buying a tool? None of this needs procurement. A spreadsheet, a shared document and four short conversations get a usable first version out the door. - **Monday.** Create the spreadsheet with those three columns. Seed it with every system already in use: the model inside the product, the support tool, the analytics dashboard that quietly added an AI summary. - **Tuesday and Wednesday.** Interview engineering, marketing, finance and support directly, not by survey. Ask each team what they actually use day to day, since a spreadsheet plug-in with a model behind it belongs on the list too. - **Thursday.** Fill in the vendor, data and risk-tier columns from what you heard. Flag anything nobody could describe clearly for a follow-up conversation rather than a guess. - **Friday.** Assign an owner to every row, pick a reviewer for the risk tiers, and put a recheck date on the calendar before anyone calls the list finished. ## What a register does not do Building the register is the easy part of this, and several harder parts of AI governance sit outside it. It does not replace a lawyer's read of a vendor contract. The register tells legal which vendor to check and what data reaches them. It says nothing about whether that vendor's specific contract terms are safe to sign. Those terms change often enough that last year's answer will not do. The registration duty in the [EU AI Act](/glossary/eu-ai-act) is a separate, public step for certain high-risk systems. It means registering under Article 49, in the database the Commission set up under Article 71, before the system goes live. An internal register is how you find out fast which systems might owe that separate duty; it is not a substitute for filing it. It does not stay accurate on its own, either. A register nobody owns drifts out of date within a quarter, and a stale register reads to a reviewer as no register at all. If you would rather someone else run the discovery and the first risk pass, an [AI Readiness & Risk Assessment](/services/ai-readiness-and-risk-assessment) does the same work in two weeks. It also hands you a finished register. The [starter kit](/resources/ai-governance-starter-kit) lists the register with the other documents a security review asks for.

rows.text: This page starts from what is required, then asks what the evidence supports. The [AI operating model](/glossary/ai-operating-model) here is the one the glossary defines. What the law requires about structure is narrow, and the dates are still moving. What the evidence supports is long and weak. ## Does any law require an AI committee or a Chief AI Officer? For a private company, no source reviewed for this page requires any of four things. They are a committee, a centre of excellence, a hub-and-spoke model and a Chief AI Officer. The European Commission's [AI literacy Q&A](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/ai-literacy-questions-answers) asks whether an AI officer is necessary, as under the GDPR. It also asks whether an organisation must set up an [AI governance](/glossary/ai-governance) board. The answer is "No, no specific governance structure is mandated to comply with article 4 of the AI Act." That answer covers Article 4 only. The one binding rule found for this page that does require such structures is American. [OMB's memo on federal AI use](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/M-25-21-Accelerating-Federal-Use-of-AI-through-Innovation-Governance-and-Public-Trust.pdf), dated 3 April 2025, tells each federal agency to name a Chief AI Officer. Each agency covered by the CFO Act must also convene an AI governance board. Even there, agencies "are permitted to rely on existing governance bodies." The memo binds US federal agencies and nobody else. The standards read the same way. The [NIST AI RMF](/glossary/nist-ai-rmf) is voluntary. Its [published text](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/nist.ai.100-1.pdf) calls it "use-case agnostic, providing flexibility to organizations of all sizes." It prescribes no committee or team shape. [ISO/IEC 42001](/glossary/iso-iec-42001) applies to "any organization, regardless of size." Its contents list roles, responsibilities and authorities. The standard is sold, not published, so its clause text was not read for this page. ## What does the law require instead? In the Articles reviewed here, the [EU AI Act](/glossary/eu-ai-act) asks for duties, not structures. Which duties apply depends on what a company does with AI. It also depends on whether the company is the [provider or the deployer](/glossary/provider-vs-deployer) of each system. The table lists the duties of the Articles reviewed, by trigger, using the [consolidated text](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/2026-07-27/eng). The [Digital Omnibus](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1744/oj/eng), Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, rewrote some of the wording and moved the dates in July 2026. The last column is a reading of what each duty needs in practice. It is not law text. | If your company… | The duty | Applies from | What it needs in practice | | --------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Provides or deploys any AI system | Article 4: take measures to support the AI literacy of staff and others who use AI for you. No specific level is required. | In application since 2 February 2025. National authorities enforce from 2 August 2026. | Someone to run the measures. The Commission says there is no need for a certificate and that organisations can keep an internal record of trainings. | | Runs a chatbot or generates synthetic content | Article 50: transparency duties for providers and deployers of chatbots, generative systems and deepfake content. Providers of generative systems must mark outputs in a machine-readable format. | 2 August 2026. Generative systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 have until 2 December 2026 to mark. | An owner for disclosure wording, and for marking if you provide the system. | | Provides a [high-risk AI system](/glossary/high-risk-ai-system) | Article 17: a documented quality management system with an accountability framework. It sets out the responsibilities of management and other staff. It must fit the size of the provider. | 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems. 2 August 2028 for Annex I systems. | A written accountability framework. | | Deploys a high-risk AI system | Article 26: give [human oversight](/glossary/human-oversight) to people with "the necessary competence, training and authority". Also monitor the system, keep logs for six months or more, and report risks. | The same two dates. | Named overseers. The Act leaves the deployer "freedom to organise its own resources and activities". | | Changes a system someone else built | Article 25: a deployer becomes the provider if it puts its own name on a high-risk system or changes it substantially. The same happens if it changes a system's purpose so that it becomes high-risk. | No start date for Article 25 in the sources reviewed. | A change-control step that decides when the role flips. | Look at what these duties name. They name an accountability framework (Article 17) and people with the competence, training and authority for human oversight (Article 26). None names a committee, a centre of excellence or a Chief AI Officer. In practice, Article 4 needs someone to run the literacy measures and Article 50 needs an owner for disclosure wording; that is a reading, not law text. The Commission adds that, for deployers of high-risk systems, the duty to train staff for human oversight "remains in place" alongside Article 4. I deliver the Article 4 literacy measures for clients. Each role gets a short session built for that role and a one-page list of dos and don'ts. The client signs the internal record. ### How firm are the EU dates? The omnibus was signed on 8 July 2026 and is in force from 27 July. It moved the high-risk dates to 2 December 2027 (Annex III systems) and 2 August 2028 (Annex I systems). Its preamble gives the reason: "the delayed availability of standards, common specifications, and alternative guidance and the delayed establishment of national competent authorities." It also rewrote Article 4 and Article 17(2). Treat the new dates with care. The omnibus dates from July 2026, and several Commission guidelines are still pending, so the practical detail is still to come. I plan client work against the dates recorded on this page: Annex III from 2 December 2027 and Annex I from 2 August 2028. I do not put dates in contracts. Company size also changes the exposure to fines. Small and medium-sized companies pay the lower of the two fine limits. The omnibus extends that rule to small mid-cap companies, a new size class just above them, for all but the highest tier. ## Who decides, and who answers? This page treats five decisions as ones that need a named owner; that is the writer's reading, not a finding of any source. The table sets what law and standards say about each against what surveys report. The last table in the next section gives the sample behind each survey. | Decision | What law and standards say | What organisations report | | ------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Approve a system for production | NIST asks executive leadership to take responsibility for decisions about AI risk (GOVERN 2.3). It prescribes no committee or team shape. | The Bank of England and FCA surveyed 118 firms in 2024. 72% give accountability for AI use cases to executive leadership. Most name three or more accountable people or bodies. | | Own the evaluation | NIST MEASURE 1.3: internal experts who did not build the system, or independent assessors, join regular assessments. | No source reviewed says who should own an evaluation set after handover at a company of this size. | | Sign risk acceptance | NIST asks for residual risk to be documented. It names no signer, and neither do the AI Act articles reviewed. | The US federal memo names one: a waiver of its requirements for high-impact AI needs a written determination by the agency's Chief AI Officer. | | Keep the inventory | NIST GOVERN 1.6 asks for mechanisms to inventory AI systems. | ASIC found some licensees with no AI inventory and others with several dispersed model registers. | | Run it after launch | AI Act Article 26: deployers of high-risk systems monitor them, keep logs for six months or more and report risks. | A 2025 survey sponsored by Pacific AI found that 48% of organisations monitor production AI systems. It gives no clear figure for companies of this size. | In the table, NIST speaks to four of these decisions and AI Act Article 26 to the fifth. Of the texts reviewed, no NIST subcategory names an approver, NIST names no risk-acceptance signer and the AI Act articles reviewed name none. Practice varies too. The IAPP and Credo AI report says: "There is no clear best practice for how to build and organize an AI governance team." ASIC describes better and poorer practice for a committee where one exists. It describes better practice as a cross-functional, executive-level committee with clear responsibility and decision-making authority. The [register post](/blog/how-to-build-an-ai-system-register-in-a-week) shows how to keep one. ## Which structures do companies use, and how good is the evidence? Every respondent was a Chief AI Officer, so each already had a central AI leader. IBM adds that organisations generally move from decentralised models to centralised or hub-and-spoke models as they scale. No source reviewed measures this against the others or separates it from decentralised. | Popular. One case story. | | Champions network | Named people in teams who spot issues. | Microsoft runs Responsible AI Champs. The sources also disagree about where authority should sit. IBM and Gartner lean central. MIT NANDA leans local for implementation. They may describe different layers: central for policy and risk, local for finding use cases. No source tests that reading. I take no public side on centralised versus decentralised. ## Where do the switch-point numbers come from? No data was found behind any of them: the one vendor page read in full cites no data for its numbers, and the other two were seen only as search snippets. One page also puts a figure on rework. The three vendor thresholds found have no data behind them. No source reviewed reports a cost for any structure in headcount, budget or time. My own switch point has no number. The structure grows when the queue of decisions outruns what one named owner can review. One ASIC finding is about the order of events. It says the CEO may take that role in a smaller organisation. It also says "There is not a single correct answer to these questions." Its papers show what advisers agree on, not what has been shown to work. Parts of the law scale with size too. Article 17(2) ties a provider's quality management system to the size of its organisation. It also asks for a senior leader as the overall owner and a specific person accountable for every system. ## How do you choose? The evidence cannot pick a structure for you. It can narrow the choice. Decide for each AI system whether your company is the provider or the deployer, and whether the system is high-risk. That decides which dates apply. 2. Name an owner for each of the five decisions. Pick triggers from your own events, not from a vendor number. Review the structure when a duty date arrives, when you add a high-risk system, after an incident, or when use grows faster than the controls. 5. Test the structure on your own records at a fixed date. None of the large studies reports results for a company your size. Your register does. The [post on why pilots stall](/blog/why-your-ai-pilot-never-reached-production) shows what happens when step two is skipped. Write the five names down first. Then see whether any duty above needs more than that. ## What do these sources leave out? They cannot say which structure produces better results at a company this size. None of the large studies reports results for companies of 30 to 300 people. They give no cost for any structure. Most are dated 2023 to 2026; Microsoft's account of its own programme is from 2021, and two pages carry no date. Some of the data is older than the omnibus. Agentic systems are a gap. No regulator text or standard reviewed assigns decision rights to an AI agent. The Australian guidance still says to name a person accountable for every system. Standards are moving too. NIST says its framework "is being updated", so every subcategory cited here comes from the January 2023 text.

rows.text: There is no standard multi-agent reference architecture in the sources reviewed here. What exists is vendor guidance from Microsoft, Google Cloud, AWS and Anthropic. In my reading, it repeats four ideas: a coordinating agent routes work, tools sit behind one controlled boundary, state lives outside the model, and every call is logged against a named identity. On whether several agents beat one, the disagreement is between Anthropic and Cognition, not among the clouds. Anthropic reports gains from its own multi-agent research system on breadth-first queries. Cognition argued in 2025 against agents working together, and in April 2026 said its observations still hold for parallel writers. A Google Research study found results from large gains to large losses, depending on the task. Production work needs limits on every run, state that survives a crash, and a trace of every call. It needs approval for high-impact actions, versioned changes with a way back, and one accountable person. The sources back these unevenly, and the table grades the points that matter most.
