rows.text: Microsoft, Google Cloud and AWS each publish guidance on multi-agent systems. The guidance is useful, and it agrees on more than you might expect. It is also vendor guidance with little measured evidence behind it. In my reading it says least about limits, rollback and ownership. This page grades the main claims and says plainly where the research found nothing. A multi-agent system, in these sources, puts several agents on one task. Each agent is a model with its own instructions and tools. One agent usually coordinates the rest. The sources call it an orchestrator, a supervisor, a coordinator, a manager agent or a lead agent. This page says orchestrator. The [agentic workflow](/glossary/agentic-workflow) entry in the glossary covers the wider idea. Outside claims name their source, and a date where the page has one. I read each page on 2 October 2026, except the Gartner release. Gartner blocks scripted reads, so I checked its sentences on a reproduction. Several of the pages change often. Where I write that I found no source, I mean none among the sources I read. A miss does not prove nobody says it elsewhere. ## How far can each claim be trusted? Treat most of it as advice. Almost none of it was measured in a production workload. The table grades the points that matter most, and the sections after it give the detail. | Point | What the sources show | How far to trust it | | -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | One agent or several | Anthropic (13 June 2025) reports gains from its multi-agent research system. Cognition (12 June 2025) argued against agents working together. On 22 April 2026 it said its observations still hold for parallel writers. | Each is one vendor's own work. I found no source that compares both in a production workload. | | Test failure rates | A NeurIPS 2025 paper (revised 26 October 2025) found failure rates from 41% to 86.7% across seven open-source frameworks. | Peer reviewed. It tested open-source frameworks, not production systems with an eval gate. | | Cancelled projects | Gartner (25 June 2025) forecasts that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027. | A forecast. The release leans on a poll of 3,412 webinar attendees. | | Runaway loops | Anthropic says early versions spawned 50 subagents for simple queries. A preprint (2 July 2026) found loop-prone code in 47 projects. | Not found: a dated, checkable post-mortem from production. The only accounts found repeat one set of figures with no primary record. | | Human approval | Anthropic (25 May 2026) says users approved roughly 93% of permission prompts. Microsoft (4 June 2026) calls bypass of the human step the most consistently exploited failure mode. | Each is the vendor's own finding. Anthropic's post gives no method for its figure. | | Evals in CI | Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework (3 December 2025) and Anthropic's evals post (9 January 2026) say to run evaluations in CI/CD pipelines. | Two primary sources among the pages searched. A practice, not a standard. | | Rollback speed | Microsoft says "immediate". Temporal says "instant". | Not found: a target time in any source reviewed. | ## Do the big vendors agree on a shape? My reading is mostly yes, on four ideas. A coordinating agent routes work to others. Tool access goes through one controlled boundary. State lives outside the model. Every call is logged against a named identity. The guides do not all say all four, but each idea recurs. Microsoft's [reference architecture](https://microsoft.github.io/multi-agent-reference-architecture/docs/reference-architecture/Reference-Architecture.html), last updated on 18 August 2025, has an orchestrator. It consults a classifier to route a request and a registry to find agents. It connects tools through a [Model Context Protocol](/glossary/mcp) server and keeps state in persistent storage. The [multi-agent guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/multiagent-ai-system) from Google Cloud, last reviewed on 16 September 2025, also centres on a coordinator agent. Microsoft, Google Cloud and Anthropic each advise starting small. Microsoft (12 February 2026) says to use the lowest level of complexity that reliably meets your requirements. Google Cloud (reviewed 28 May 2026) recommends starting with a single agent if you are early in agent development. Anthropic (19 December 2024, updated 10 August 2026) advises finding the simplest solution possible and adding complexity only when needed. AWS (10 June 2026) warns of coordination overhead, handoff complexity and distributed failure modes. An undated AWS Marketplace learning module, written in the first person, also recommends the simplest pattern that fits your workflow. These are companies that sell the platforms. The Microsoft and Google Cloud pages quoted above report no measured data. Their agreement tells you what the vendors advise. ## Should the default be one agent or several? Start with one. Microsoft, Google Cloud and Anthropic each advise starting small, and the sources still disagree about what comes next. Two of the sources landed a day apart, and my reading is that they disagree on where the line sits. Cognition, which makes the Devin coding agent, published ["Don't Build Multi-Agents"](https://cognition.com/blog/dont-build-multi-agents) on 12 June 2025. Anthropic described its [multi-agent research system](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system) on 13 June 2025. Cognition wrote that "in 2025, running multiple agents in collaboration only results in fragile systems." One of its principles was to share context. Anthropic says its research system "uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern". A lead agent coordinates specialised subagents that run in parallel. Anthropic's own evaluations show that such systems "excel especially for breadth-first queries". I read that as a read-heavy task, graded by the vendor itself. Cognition came back to the question on 22 April 2026. Its original observations, it wrote, "still hold today for parallel-writer swarms". It also described a narrower pattern that works, in which several agents add intelligence to a task while "writes stay single-threaded". The same post gives two rules that pull apart. One says to "share as much context as possible between the agents". For review agents, it says the technique works best when the coding and review agents "do not share any context beforehand". My default puts the line between reading and writing. Many independent reads suit several agents. Writes that must agree suit one. I found no source that tested this in a production workload. The closest measurement found is a Google Research study of agent designs on benchmark tasks. Its [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.08296), posted on 9 December 2025 and revised on 8 April 2026, compared several designs with a single agent. Results ran from a gain of 80.8% to a loss of 70.0%, depending on the task. The Google Research blog post about the paper, of 28 January 2026, reports that independent agents amplified errors 17.2 times, and centralised ones 4.4 times. The blog counts fewer test configurations than the paper's latest abstract, so the paper changed after the blog. I cannot say the multipliers hold for the paper. Anthropic's own post says multi-agent systems "work mainly because they help spend enough tokens to solve the problem". One reading is that more tokens help, however they are spent. I found no source that separates the gain from structure from the gain from extra tokens. ## What do the failure studies show? Multi-agent systems fail often in tests, and the studies below do not show how often they fail in production. One is MAST, from Cemri and colleagues, accepted to the NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks track. It read the traces of seven open-source multi-agent frameworks and found [failure rates from 41% to 86.7%](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.13657). Repeated steps and agents that miss a finished task were among the common failures. The paper is peer reviewed. It tested open-source frameworks, not production systems with an eval gate in front of them. A runaway loop is a different case, because it costs money. The research found no dated, checkable post-mortem of one in production. The only accounts I found were blog posts that repeat one set of figures with no primary record. What I found is weaker. Anthropic says early versions of its research system made errors such as spawning 50 subagents for simple queries. A [preprint of 2 July 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01641), "When Agents Do Not Stop", scanned public agent repositories for code that can start an infinite loop. It counts code patterns and does not show a loop that ran in production. My own case is the one first-hand example here: a runaway loop in client work, with no client named. An automatic stop ended it: a step limit and a cost ceiling. The account is anonymised. Hijacking is another documented failure. NIST's CAISI tested agent hijacking on a public benchmark. The strongest new attack succeeded 81% of the time, against 11% for the strongest baseline attack. [NIST published the result](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2025/01/technical-blog-strengthening-ai-agent-hijacking-evaluations) on 17 January 2025 and updated it on 19 December 2025. That is a benchmark, so it shows what is possible. It gives no rate for real systems. NIST's wording is that many agents that read untrusted text are open to [prompt injection](/glossary/prompt-injection). ## Where do limits and cost controls belong? On every run, set by a person, with a defined result when the limit is reached. The defaults in popular frameworks differ, and they count different things. The table shows five frameworks as read on 2 October 2026. The OpenAI default comes from its source code on GitHub, and the other rows from documentation pages. | Framework | Default loop limit | What it counts | | ---------------------------- | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | | OpenAI Agents SDK | 10 | Turns of the agent loop in one run. Setting none removes the limit. | | LangGraph | 1,000 | Steps, since version 1.0.6. | | Microsoft Agent Framework | 100 | Iterations of a workflow run toward convergence. | | Google Agent Development Kit | None stated | A loop agent ends on a stop signal or on a maximum you set. | | Claude Agent SDK | No limit unless set | The docs advise setting a budget for production agents. | A turn, a step and an iteration are different units, so in my reading the three numbers cannot be compared. Step limits and cost limits are also separate controls. I give every run a step limit. A run that reaches it stops, an alert goes out, and a person decides whether it resumes. I print no numbers. The Claude Agent SDK documentation says the loop runs until Claude finishes if you set no limits. It calls a budget a good default for production agents. The [FAQ on cost per outcome](/faq/how-is-cost-per-outcome-measured) gives this site's definition of the measure, and I would set a ceiling from your own traces. ## Does an agent need durable state and traces? Yes, the sources say both. State has to survive a crash, and every call needs a trace. Anthropic's [managed agents post](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/managed-agents) of 8 April 2026 keeps the session log outside the process that runs the agent. Nothing in that process has to survive a crash. Temporal, which sells durable execution, says its service hands the work to another process after a crash and rebuilds the state. LangGraph's documentation says in-memory checkpoints are lost when the process restarts, and it recommends a durable checkpointer. The principle is well supported. I found no source that says every production agent needs a separate engine, and none that measures the benefit. Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework (3 December 2025) says to attribute every action to a specific agent instance and conversation ID. The OpenTelemetry conventions for agent spans were still marked as in development in the repository file read on 2 October 2026. Whether the core traces signal is stable is unconfirmed, so this page makes no claim about it. Two primary sources say it: Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework and Anthropic's evals post, which calls automated evals especially useful pre-launch and in CI/CD. The Microsoft Cloud Adoption Framework says to integrate evaluations into CI/CD pipelines before production. I set the threshold on the first run against historical data, and it only rises, never falls. The owner can override a block, in writing in the pull request. ## Who approves what, and who owns the system? A person should approve high-impact actions, and one named person should own the system. AWS sorts actions into three tiers, autonomous, notify and approve, by impact and reversibility, so that not every action waits for a person. Approval is also a control that can fail. Anthropic reports that its telemetry showed users approved roughly 93% of permission prompts (25 May 2026). It adds that the more approvals a user sees, the less attention each one gets. rows.text: An AI pilot never reached production because of an organisational gap, not a technical one. A demo only has to impress the person running it. Production has to survive a change of prompt, a change of model and a change of the person who built it. It has to do that without anyone noticing except a number on a dashboard. Six conditions decide whether that gap closes. One named owner still answers for the system a year after launch. A data classification signed off by someone with authority says what a vendor may see. An outcome number moves when the system works, matched by an eval that runs in the build pipeline before every release. Tracing shows which step produced a bad answer, and a rollback fires on a threshold, not an argument. Most stalled pilots are missing the first two, and a team cannot build the rest until those exist.

rows.text: A pilot stalls in the space between working once and working every time. Most proof-of-concepts skip four things production always needs. Two of them are a named owner who still answers a year after launch and a decision about which data may leave the building. The other two are a number that says whether the system is working, and an automatic check that catches a regression before a customer does. ## Where do pilots actually stop? ### Nobody owns the risk Pilots are usually built by whoever was curious enough to try. That person is rarely still around, or still in charge, once the project needs a decision about risk. Nobody has the standing to say the system is ready, and nobody has to explain a bad output to a customer or a regulator. Ownership means one name attached to the outcome, with the budget and the authority to pause the system if it misbehaves. A shared inbox or a Slack channel does not count. Without that name, every stall becomes permanent, because nobody is accountable for unsticking it. ### Legal has not said which data may leave Most pilots reach a vendor's API before anyone has classified the data going into the prompt. That is fine for a demo running on sample records. It stops a rollout the moment a security review asks what customer data the system touches and where it goes. The NIST AI RMF treats this as a governance decision under its Govern function, not a technical detail to settle after launch. Without a data classification written down in advance, every new use case reopens the same argument with legal. The pilot waits on a decision nobody has been asked to make yet. ### There is no measurable outcome A pilot that nobody can prove is working also cannot be proven to be failing, which is worse. Teams show accuracy on a curated test set, or a handful of good transcripts. Nobody has picked the business number the system is meant to move. Examples are tickets resolved, hours saved or the error rate on a defined task. Without that number, a debate about whether to invest further has no evidence on either side. The safest move for everyone involved is to let the pilot run quietly forever, rather than kill it or fund it properly. ### Nobody would notice a regression Prompts change, the underlying model changes on a provider's own schedule, and traffic drifts. Pilots rarely have a way to detect when any of that makes the output worse. There is no test suite running against real examples before a change ships. So a regression appears first as a customer complaint or a bad downstream decision, not as a failed build. That is the opposite of how the rest of the engineering organisation ships software. This gap is usually the reason a platform or security review declines to sign off. ## What has to be true to ship? Six conditions turn a pilot into something a platform team will actually run. None of them are exotic. Most engineering teams already do the equivalent for every other production system they own. | Condition | What it means in practice | What its absence looks like | | ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | An owner. | One named person, on the team that runs the system, with authority to pause it. | No one can explain a bad output, so the stall becomes permanent. | | A data classification. | A written answer, agreed with whoever owns data risk, on what a vendor may store. | Every new use case reopens the same argument with legal. | | A measurable outcome. | One number the business already tracks, with a floor the system must clear. | Nobody can prove the pilot works, so it runs quietly forever instead of shipping or dying. | | Evals in CI. | Real test cases run on every prompt or model change; OWASP treats this as baseline hygiene. | A regression reaches a customer before anyone on the team sees it. | | Tracing and cost per outcome. | Every run logged well enough to reconstruct, with a cost a finance team can read. | Nobody can say what a run costs, or which step produced a bad answer. | | Rollback. | A rehearsed way to revert to the last prompt, model or version within minutes. | The team improvises during the first real incident instead of using a tested path. | For a system that touches decisions about people, the EU AI Act sets a similar bar for higher-risk uses. It requires a documented risk-management process, records that make a decision traceable and a human who can step in. Meeting the six conditions above gets most of the way there even for teams the Act does not yet cover. ## How would I sequence it? I run this as one pass, not six parallel workstreams, because the six conditions above depend on each other. You cannot set a rollback threshold before you have a measured outcome, and you cannot classify data before someone owns the decision to do it. ### Pick one process Choose a single workflow with enough volume to matter and an outcome you can measure without a survey, not five pilots running at once. An AI readiness and risk assessment is the fastest way to get that choice onto paper. Two weeks of reading the existing systems and vendor list end in a memo. The memo names an owner candidate, a first data classification and the number the process should move. ### Build it in ninety days A 90-Day Production Sprint turns that memo into a running system. Evals get written alongside the first working version, rather than bolted on at the end. Tracing and cost per outcome go live on a dashboard from week one. The rollback path gets rehearsed before real traffic arrives, not during the first incident. ### Hand it to someone who was in the room The internal owner should have written at least one eval case and watched the rollback rehearsal, so the runbook describes a system they already understand. A handover document given to someone who was not part of the build is a liability with a due date, not a transfer of knowledge. ## What this does not solve This sequence gets one process into production with the six conditions in place. Several harder governance questions stay outside it. Your risk appetite is still your call, not this sequence's. Two companies with the same pilot and the same data can reasonably choose different answers about what a vendor may see. That decision belongs to whoever owns risk at your company, not something a framework or an outside advisor can make for you. It does not replace a legal review of your contracts with model vendors. Classifying data tells your lawyers what question to ask. It does not answer whether a specific vendor's terms are acceptable, and that answer changes as vendors change their terms. The underlying model is exactly as reliable as it was before this sequence started. Evals catch regressions against the cases you thought to test. They do not catch every way a general-purpose model can fail on a case nobody wrote down. That is why the rollback path matters as much as the evals do. It does not scale to five processes at once. The sequence above is built for one workflow with one owner. Running it for a second or third process repeats the same ninety days. It does not shortcut them.

rows.text: ## What this is A panel specification for tracking how AI tools are used at work. It has eight panels. Each names the question it answers, the data source and the decision it supports. It is a page, not a dashboard file. You copy the panels into whatever tool you already run. Version 0.1 covers coding assistants and chat assistants. Version 0.2 will cover SaaS tools with AI built in and internal agents. I will write it when clients who run them appear. The panels fall into three kinds. rows.text: ## What this is A CI workflow and an eval case format for one [agentic workflow](/glossary/agentic-workflow). The same discipline sits inside the [90-Day Production Sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint). A prompt or model change should not merge without passing a test set first. ## The eval case format | Field | Purpose | Example | | -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | | id | A stable name, so a failure is traceable across runs | refund-double-charge | | input | The exact prompt or tool call the agent receives | Customer says they were charged twice | | expected | A pass rule: an exact match, a check, or a second model acting as a grader | Refund issued, ticket closed, no invented apology | | tags | The failure mode a case guards against | prompt-injection, tool-misuse, refusal | ## The CI gate The workflow runs the eval set on every pull request, scores it, and blocks the merge under your floor. Nobody has to remember to run it by hand, which is the part that fails first once a team is busy. The tags borrow their shape from [OWASP's Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications](https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-for-large-language-model-applications/). Prompt injection and excessive agency (the agent doing something nobody asked it to) appear in a support agent as often as in a public chatbot. A tagged case catches the regression either way. ## What it is not It is not a considered eval set on its own. A handful of cases pulled from real conversations tests more than a long list invented at a desk. The starter takes no position on which cases you pick. Choosing the cases still maps to the MEASURE function (one of the framework's four functions) in [NIST's AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework).

rows.text: ## What this is The four documents that answer most of a corporate security review. They are deliberately short: a register nobody updates is worse than no register. The kit also sets out the order in which to call people when an AI system fails. ## What it is not It is not a compliance certificate, and it is not legal advice. It is the paperwork a reviewer expects to see before they look at your architecture. ## Who signs what | Document | What it's for | Who signs it | | ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | | AI register | Every AI system in use, who owns it, what data reaches it. | The named AI risk owner keeps it current. | | Acceptable-use policy | What you may paste into a tool, and what you may not. | Every employee who uses an AI tool for work. | | Data classification table | Which vendors may see which tier of data. | The AI risk owner, together with whoever owns the data. | | Vendor questionnaire | One answer set procurement can reuse for every new vendor. | Procurement, before anyone signs a vendor contract. | It maps loosely to what ISO/IEC 42001 and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) both expect a company to have on file. It does not require either. ## Vendor questionnaire The other three documents describe how you handle AI. This one asks each vendor how it handles your data. Send the same questions to every AI vendor, and file the answers with the contract. The questions cover these topics: - Whether the vendor trains models on your data, and how you opt out. - Where your data is processed and stored, who at the vendor can read it, and which [sub-processors](/glossary/sub-processor) touch it. - How the vendor announces a model change, and whether you can stay on a fixed version. - How the vendor tells you about an incident, and who answers when you call. - Whether the system counts as high-risk under the [EU AI Act](/glossary/eu-ai-act), and which duties the contract leaves with you. - What happens to your data and prompts when the contract ends. ## Incident response plan When an AI system fails, its owner should not have to work out who to call. Write this call order down beside the register, with a name and a backup against each role. Inside the company, in this order: 1. The system owner named in the register, who limits or stops the system and keeps its logs and model version as they were. 2. The AI risk owner, who decides whether the incident is serious. 3. An executive who can approve a report and a message to customers. 4. Legal counsel, and whoever handles data breaches if personal data is involved. Outside the company, in this order: 5. The provider of the system, which is often the vendor. 6. The importer or distributor, if the system has one. 7. The market surveillance authority. 8. Affected customers, as your contracts require. For a high-risk system you deploy, Article 26 of the EU AI Act asks the deployer to give notice at once when it identifies a serious incident. The order is the provider first, then the importer or distributor and the market surveillance authority. Log the time each person learned of the incident. The page on [serious incident reporting](/glossary/serious-incident-reporting) says which moment starts the clock for a report and sets out the deadlines, so this plan does not repeat them.

rows.text: ## What this is Five axes, scored from zero to three, that give you a rough position before you pay anyone to check it properly. The axes match the ones in the [AI Readiness & Risk Assessment](/services/ai-readiness-and-risk-assessment). This is the self-administered version, without the evidence behind it. ## The five axes | Axis | 0 — not started | 1 — informal | 2 — documented | 3 — evidenced | | ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------- | | Strategy | No one has named which processes to automate first | Someone has an opinion, nothing written down | A ranked shortlist exists | The shortlist is reviewed by whoever owns the budget | | Data | No one knows what a vendor tool can see | A rough sense exists, not written down | A data classification table exists | The table is checked before a new tool is approved | | Delivery | Every pilot has stalled before production | One pilot is close to live | One system is live, unmonitored | A system is live, monitored, with a rollback path | | People | Only the original builder understands any AI system in use | One other person has read the code | A second person has changed it and shipped | Ownership is written down and handed over on a schedule | | Governance | No [AI register](/glossary/ai-register) exists | A register exists, out of date | A register exists, reviewed occasionally | The register is reviewed on a fixed schedule | ## Scoring it Score each axis from zero to three using the table above, then add the five scores for a total out of fifteen. A low total early on is common. It usually means nobody has written anything down yet, not that the engineering is behind. The five axes are not a substitute for the [NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) or [ISO/IEC 42001](https://www.iso.org/standard/42001). They are a rougher pass at the same territory, built to take an afternoon rather than an audit. ## What it is not It is not the Assessment, and it carries no evidence a reviewer would accept. A self-given three is a claim until someone outside your team checks what you have actually written down.

rows.text: ## What this is A worksheet for one recurring decision: build the workflow yourself, or buy a vendor's version of it. It will not choose for you. It gives the choice a written reason, which is what a board or a buyer asks for later. ## The six criteria | Criterion | Build tends to win when | Buy tends to win when | | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- | | Data residency | Customer data cannot leave your infrastructure by contract or by law | A vendor already holds a data-processing agreement you trust | | Customisation depth | The workflow is core to what makes your product different | The workflow looks like everyone else's version of the same task | | Time to a working version | You already have the engineers and the model access | Procurement moves faster than a hiring plan would | | Total cost over years | Usage is high enough that a per-call fee compounds | Usage is uncertain, and a fixed fee caps the downside | | Exit cost | You can rebuild the model calls without rebuilding the product | A second vendor could take over most of the same job | | Ownership when it breaks | An internal team already owns the surrounding process | A vendor's contract has a real answer to who to call | ## Scoring it Weight the six criteria for your situation, score build and buy against each one, and let the total argue with your gut feeling. A bought tool still needs an owner and a place in your [AI register](/glossary/ai-register). [NIST's AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) treats a vendor's model the same as one you trained. That sits under its MAP function (one of the framework's four functions). The risk to your customer does not care who wrote the code. ## Total cost of ownership The Total cost over years criterion needs a total cost of ownership (TCO) estimate, and a vendor quote covers only part of it. Fill in the categories in the table below, for build and for buy. Use the same horizon for both sides, long enough to cover the longest contract you would sign. For each side, add what you pay once to what you pay in every period of that horizon. | Side | Cost category | What to count | | ----- | ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Build | Engineering time | Engineer hours for the first version, and the work those engineers would otherwise ship | | Build | Maintenance | Upkeep as the model API, your libraries and your product change | | Build | Drift monitoring | The [evals](/glossary/evals) and review that catch quality slipping as models and data change | | Buy | Licence | The vendor's fee in the unit they meter it, and how it grows with your usage | | Buy | Integration | Connecting the tool to your data, login and workflows, plus the security review | | Buy | Lock-in | The cost of leaving: moving data out, redoing prompts and workflows, retraining staff | Take every amount from your own quotes and payroll, because this page lists no amounts. Use the same usage forecast on both sides, since the criteria table above shows that usage often decides which side costs less. Lock-in is the cost behind the Exit cost criterion, so fill in both together. ## What it is not It is not a procurement process, and it will not pick the vendor for you. It decides one thing: whether the job belongs inside your codebase or inside someone else's product. This is the call the [Fractional CAIO Retainer](/services/fractional-caio-retainer) reviews every quarter, alongside the [shadow AI](/glossary/shadow-ai) a team already bought without asking.

rows.text: ## What this is The Handover Playbook is a plan to fill in, not a finished one. It moves AI leadership from an outside lead to a named person inside your company. Most rows ask for a name, a place or a date; the rest ask for a decision. Only your company knows those. The reasons for each table, and how much weight each source carries, are in [How to hand over AI leadership to an internal owner](/blog/handing-over-ai-leadership-to-an-internal-owner). ## Stage 1. The owner and the test Fill this in first. This playbook asks for a written test so that the handover can end on a result, not only on a date. The [pilot article](/blog/why-your-ai-pilot-never-reached-production) says the new owner should have written at least one eval case and watched the rollback rehearsal. The [approach page](/approach) has a related test of whether your engineers can roll back a bad model without waiting on the outside lead. My test has three checks, and I judge each one. The new owner writes an eval case and runs a rollback rehearsal. The new owner also handles one incident without me in the room. | Question | Your answer | | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------- | | Who takes the role? Write one name. | | | Who decides whether to stop a launch, if that is a different person? | | | What must the new owner do without the outside lead before the role moves? | | | Who judges each check? | | | What counts as a pass? Write it so a third person could judge it. | | | What happens if the new owner is not ready on the planned date? | | ## Stage 2. What moves My handover takes three months, in three phases. The month-one plan sets the end date, not the contract. | Phase | Months | What happens | | ----- | ------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------- | | 1 | Months one and two | The new owner and the outside lead work side by side. | | 2 | Month three | The new owner leads. The outside lead reviews. | | 3 | End of month three | The final test and the signatures. | One row per item. Fill in who holds it today, who holds it after, where it lives and the date it moved. The reason for each row comes first, and its source where it has one, so you can drop a row you disagree with. | Item | Why it is here | Held today by | Held after by | Where it lives | Done on | | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------- | ------------- | -------------- | ------- | | Decisions and their reasons | A UK regulator says handover material should include judgement and opinion, not just facts and figures. [FCA handbook](https://handbook.fca.org.uk/handbook/sysc25/sysc25s9), an analogy from financial firms. | | | | | | Work in progress | Status, owner and next action for each open item. [Fractionus](https://fractionus.com/blog/fractional-executive-offboarding), one vendor's advice. | | | | | | Open risks and concerns | The same regulator says the material should include unresolved or possible breaches and unresolved concerns raised by regulators. FCA handbook, an analogy. | | | | | | The list of AI systems | NIST asks for mechanisms to inventory AI systems. [NIST AI RMF](https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/airmf/5-sec-core/), Govern 1.6, voluntary. | | | | | | Roles and authority | NIST asks that roles, responsibilities and lines of communication are documented and clear. NIST AI RMF, Govern 2.1, voluntary. | | | | | | Runbook, evals and rollback | Google says training for a receiving team can include hands-on exercises in operations. [Google SRE book](https://sre.google/sre-book/evolving-sre-engagement-model/), the operator's own account. | | | | | | Monitoring and logs | NIST asks for monitoring plans that cover incident response and change management (Manage 4.1). For high-risk systems, deployers will have to keep the logs they control for at least six months. That duty starts on 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for Annex I systems. [Article 26](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-26) of the EU AI Act. | | | | | | Outside parties | An interim director helps announce the new leader to funders and peers. [CompassPoint](https://www.compasspoint.org/sites/default/files/documents/Interim%20EDs%20-%20final.pdf), a practitioner's guide for US nonprofits. | | | | | | Vendor and sub-processor contacts | Vendor and [sub-processor](/glossary/sub-processor) contacts are not personal. They are a row in the [AI register](/glossary/ai-register), and the renewal calendar moves with it. | | | | | ## Stage 3. Who signs what NIST AI RMF Govern 2.1 asks that roles, responsibilities and lines of communication are documented and clear. Its voluntary Playbook also suggests documenting delegated authorities. Write that down here for the handover. The rows are examples of decisions that carry a signature; no source lists them. Delete any that do not apply and add your own. For a high-risk system under the [EU AI Act](/glossary/eu-ai-act), ask counsel who must hold [human oversight](/glossary/human-oversight). | Decision | Signs today | Signs after the handover date | Change takes effect on | | ------------------------------------------- | ----------- | ----------------------------- | ---------------------- | | Entries in the AI register | | | | | Risk acceptances | | | | | Policy exceptions | | | | | Vendor and model approvals | | | | | Changes to eval thresholds | | | | | Rollback calls | | | | | Answers to customer security questionnaires | | | | | Serious incident calls | | | | ## Stage 4. Access List every account the outside lead holds. Revoke them in one coordinated step on or before the last day, and do not leave removal to the outside lead. A marketplace that sells fractional executives gives this advice and asks for written confirmation. It is one vendor's opinion. The table lists six categories of account. The client's internal owner or IT lead revokes each one, and the revocation is confirmed in writing the same day. A revoke-all line sits on the last-day checklist. | Account or system | Granted by | Revoked by | Confirmed in writing on | | ---------------------------------------- | ---------- | -------------------------------------- | ----------------------- | | The AI register | | The client's internal owner or IT lead | | | The [LLM gateway](/glossary/llm-gateway) | | The client's internal owner or IT lead | | | CI/CD | | The client's internal owner or IT lead | | | The cloud consoles | | The client's internal owner or IT lead | | | The vendor panels | | The client's internal owner or IT lead | | | The SSO admin | | The client's internal owner or IT lead | | ## Stage 5. After the last day Sources agree that some reachable help is useful and differ on how much. Agree it in writing, with its length, scope and who may call. The middle column holds my terms where I have set them. | Question | My terms | Your answer | | -------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------- | | Will the outside lead stay reachable, and for which questions? | Yes. Questions by email, answered within one working day. | | | For how long, and in what fee shape? | Thirty days after the last day, with one review call on day 30. | | | Who may call? | | | | What is out of scope after the last day? | Anything beyond the email answers and the day-30 call is a separate agreement. | | ## Stage 6. The check after handover Pick the date and the person who asks. The first question comes from one vendor's advice to ask the successor about a month after the exit. The other rows are prompts. Add your own. | Question | Date | Who asks | Answer | | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---- | -------- | ------ | | What do you wish you had known on day one? | | | | | Which decision since the handover was made without the outside lead? | | | | | Which item in the What moves table turned out to be missing? | | | | | Do customer paperwork and the AI register show the new name? | | | | ## What it is not It is not a standard. A search in October 2026 found no standard, law or study that sets out how to hand over AI leadership, and no outcome study of AI-leadership handovers. Nothing shows that these tables lead to better results. It is not legal advice, and it is not a compliance certificate. The [FAQ on how the Retainer ends](/faq/how-does-the-retainer-end) covers how the [Fractional CAIO Retainer](/services/fractional-caio-retainer) ends. No engagement has yet ended in a full handover by the method in these tables.

rows.text: ## What this is A policy file for whichever [LLM gateway](/glossary/llm-gateway) you run, hosted or self-built. It is the config, not the gateway itself. The decisions live in a file your team reviews, not in a script only one engineer remembers. ## The policy schema | Key | What it controls | Example | | -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------- | | allowed_models | Which providers and model versions a team may call | two named models, not an open list | | redact | Fields stripped before a prompt or response is logged or forwarded | email, national_id, card_number | | rate_limit | Calls per minute before the gateway queues or refuses | a ceiling per team, not per user | | log_retention | How long a request and response pair is kept | matches your data retention policy, not a default | | fallback | What happens if the primary provider is down | a named second provider, or a hard failure | ## Logging and retention The logging schema borrows its shape from [the EU AI Act's Article 12](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ%3AL_202401689), which requires automatic event logs for high-risk systems. Not every call through a gateway is high-risk. The habit costs little to build in now. It is expensive to retrofit once a regulator or a customer asks first. The `allowed_models` and `log_retention` keys map to two [NIST SP 800-53](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/53/r5/upd1/final) control families: Access Control and Audit and Accountability. Procurement questionnaires often draw on this catalogue, even when nobody names it. ## What it is not It is not a gateway, and it will not stop a determined engineer from calling a model directly. It makes an unrouted call a [shadow AI](/glossary/shadow-ai) finding. That is the layer the [90-Day Production Sprint](/services/90-day-production-sprint) puts in front of a workflow before it counts as production.

rows.text: ## What this is Two weeks. I interview the people doing the work and read your systems and your vendor list. I write one memo you can hand to a board or a customer. ## What you keep You keep one document, whether or not you continue. It holds the readiness score, the gap list, and the three processes ranked by what automating them is worth this quarter. ## ISO/IEC 42001 gap assessment The gap list compares your company with [ISO/IEC 42001](/glossary/iso-iec-42001), the standard for an AI management system that an accredited body can certify. It shows where you fall short of what the standard asks. This is a gap assessment, not a certification. An accredited body runs the independent audit that grants certification, and the [certification FAQ](/faq/can-you-get-us-iso-iec-42001-certified-or-just-a-working-system) covers the difference between a working system and a certificate. ## Why it is two weeks and not two days A readiness claim you cannot show evidence for is worth nothing in a security review. I read the code, talk to the people who use the tools, and check what your vendors actually do with your data. Two weeks is the shortest span in which I can do all three.

A three hundred person company does not need a committee, a maturity model or a consultant to run a workshop. It needs four things that fit on a shared drive and get updated when something changes.

rows.text: Choice comes first, and it is mostly a filter. A candidate process needs volume, a measurable outcome, and a tolerable failure mode. Volume, because a system used twice a week never accumulates enough signal to improve. A measurable outcome, because a metric you have to survey for cannot gate a release. A tolerable failure mode, because the first version will be wrong sometimes and you need to know what that costs.

rows.text: Adoption telemetry for AI tools usually reports seats, logins, active users and prompts. That is an inference from the sources cited here. None of them shows any of those counts predicting a business result. Self-reports can mislead too. In METR's 2025 trial, 16 experienced developers expected a 24% speed-up. Afterwards they believed they had been 20% faster. Their tasks took 19% longer. METR now marks that result out of date. In an NBER working paper issued in February 2026, nearly 6,000 senior executives reported that 69% of firms use AI. Nine in ten reported no impact on employment or productivity over three years. That is also self-report. A smaller set is easier to defend: coverage, retention by team, one agreed outcome, delivery health, cost per outcome and a trust survey read as opinion. That set is a synthesis, not a finding any source states. Collect it by team, and screen any per-person view first.

rows.text: My handover takes three months, in three phases. In months one and two, the new owner and I work side by side. In month three, the new owner leads and I review. At the end of month three come the final test and the signatures. The end date is fixed in the month-one plan, not the contract.

rows.text: Microsoft, Google Cloud and AWS each publish guidance on multi-agent systems. The guidance is useful, and it agrees on more than you might expect. It is also vendor guidance with little measured evidence behind it. In my reading it says least about limits, rollback and ownership. This page grades the main claims and says plainly where the research found nothing.

rows.text: A multi-agent system, in these sources, puts several agents on one task. Each agent is a model with its own instructions and tools. One agent usually coordinates the rest. The sources call it an orchestrator, a supervisor, a coordinator, a manager agent or a lead agent. This page says orchestrator. The agentic workflow entry in the glossary covers the wider idea.

rows.text: Multi-agent systems fail often in tests, and the studies below do not show how often they fail in production. rows.text: The Model Context Protocol specification (revision 28 July 2026) says there should always be a human in the loop who can deny tool invocations. AWS sorts actions into three tiers, autonomous, notify and approve, by impact and reversibility, so that not every action waits for a person.

rows.text: Pinning a model does not always pin behaviour. Anthropic’s documentation says infrastructure updates occasionally produce minor differences in observable behaviour even when the model ID and weights have not changed. I read that as follows: rolling back the model ID does not always roll back behaviour. Evals run after a rollback are how you would see the difference.

rows.text: A DPIA, or data protection impact assessment, is a written GDPR review completed before a company begins personal-data processing likely to carry high privacy risk. It assesses what data the company collects, why, and how the company reduces that risk. It differs from a fairness review of the system's decision.

rows.text: GDPR Article 35 makes this review mandatory, not a judgement call, in three situations. One is large-scale profiling with legal or similarly significant effects. Another is large-scale processing of special-category data, such as health or biometric records. The third is systematic large-scale monitoring of a public space. Most consequential AI systems land in the first of these by default.

rows.text: Direct injection comes from whoever is typing into the box, phrased to override the model's own hidden starting instructions, its system prompt.
